why: C spells out the setup as a list and uses full sentences, B is the same content as a sentence, A opens with a fragment ('The facts the later tasks pin, measured on...').
All three are the identical bare heading, so the order is arbitrary.
C writes out the failure case and the Windows substitution as sentences and gives Chromium its own bullet; A compresses the failure case to 'None found:' which reads as a fragment.
C reorders the newest-version warning so the instruction comes before the reason and splits the install/prefer sentence; A and B are identical and slightly denser.
A labels cause, measurement, consequences and fix and keeps the consequences as sub-bullets, so the reader sees the structure at once; B folds the consequences into one run-on bullet.
C names Helium and says 'on one of ten queries' and 'for the user to decide'; B starts with a bare 'It' after the heading, making the subject a guess.
A says 'all three match', 'which rejects everything' and splits the Helium loading into a clear sentence; B and C compress those into parentheticals, C most tersely.
B says 'hides that tab' and 'nothing needs to be preset'; C's 'hides it' leaves the referent of 'it' to be inferred.

B states the subject ('A consent wall was seen...') and spells out the causal links ('because the rule list is fetched first'); C's 'Its search page I only ever saw as /sorry' is an awkward inversion.
A names 'config files', links the control run's cause and effect with 'so', and says 'per the controller'; C's 'Control without --config:' is a terse label the outside reader must unpack.

B writes each observation as full sentences ('5 of 5 times', 'either wait ... or retry once', socket dir as its own sentence); C compresses to 'With a 1 s gap: 5 of 5 fine' and 'the first in a session 2–5 s'.
The three differ only in the Brave sentence; C's 'On Brave, &lang=de...' reads as prose, B's 'while' links the two tests, A's 'Brave:' label is the tersest.
B is a full sentence with 'engines', 'queries', 'times' and 'see below'; A drops those words so '3 blocks in 10' and '(below)' need inference.
B's intro is a sentence naming what each query ran as and what the fresh profile applied to; A and C open with a comma-joined fragment, and C also drops the comma after 'Per R8'.

B labels DuckDuckGo's three parts, says 'because Brave never showed either', 'classify both as Captcha' and 'It is not a block marker'; A's 'the parser must call both Captcha' and its bracketed DuckDuckGo list are terser and less explicit.

B bullets the scrubbed values and makes the marker sentence unambiguous ('None of the scrubbed values is a parser marker'); A packs the scrubbing into one dense paragraph and 'No parser marker lives in any of them' can be read as 'in any fixture'.
